claims.claim: Wolfe describes Kay's subject as the negotiation between story as history represents it and story as fantasy transforms it.
claims.source: Gary K. Wolfe, "Guy Gavriel Kay: An Introduction", Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 20.2 (2009)
claims.quote: between story as represented in history and story as transformed by fantasy

claims.feature: other: fantasy as a method for history
claims.claim: Kay tells the ICFA audience that his address will connect his argument about privacy to a defence of fantasy literature as a way of writing about history.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, "The Fiction of Privacy: Fantasy and the Past", Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 20.2 (2009)
claims.quote: a defense of fantasy literature as a way of addressing history

claims.feature: other: interiority of the historical dead
claims.claim: Kay rejects as nonsense the reviewer's claim that a novel can give the reader the interior world of a real person.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, "Reflections on an Ethical Society", address of 4 November 2000 (BrightWeavings, Kay's authorized site)
claims.quote: This is nonsense, and it is pervasive
claims.page: section quoting the New York Times on Oates's Blonde

claims.feature: other: the writer's licence over the recorded dead
claims.claim: Kay reports Atwood's implication that a subject's obscurity and the absence of a documentary record offer the novelist licence, and contrasts it with novelists who take the fullness of the record as conferring licence instead.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, "Reflections on an Ethical Society", address of 4 November 2000 (BrightWeavings, Kay's authorized site)
claims.quote: the absence of a record, offers license or opportunity

claims.feature: other: the writer's licence over the recorded dead
claims.claim: Kay asks whether readers should care which parts of a historical novel are real and which are invented, against reviewers who say they do not.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, "Reflections on an Ethical Society", address of 4 November 2000 (BrightWeavings, Kay's authorized site)
claims.quote: Shouldn't we care what is real and what is made up?
claims.page: section quoting the Calgary Herald on Johnson's Colony

claims.feature: other: the writer's licence over the recorded dead
claims.claim: Kay names an expanded perception of entitlement as the common element in the literary novels that use real lives.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, "Reflections on an Ethical Society", address of 4 November 2000 (BrightWeavings, Kay's authorized site)
claims.page: summary section before the closing Berra return

claims.feature: other: privacy of the ordinary person
claims.claim: Kay quotes the rabbinical formulation that the injury caused by seeing into private space cannot be measured, and takes it as the standard a society sets for itself.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, "The Fiction of Privacy: Fantasy and the Past", Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 20.2 (2009)
claims.quote: the injury caused by seeing cannot be measured

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun sets the three religions' sayings side by side and finds all three emphasise the transitory nature of things.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy", in The Light of Life: Essays in Honour of Professor Barbara Kowalik (Libron, 2017)
claims.quote: All three of them strongly emphasize the transitory nature of things

claims.feature: other: memory as the shape of the record
claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun proposes reading fantasy literature as one of the forms in which contemporary culture recalls the Middle Ages.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "Remembering the Romance", in M. J. Toswell (ed.), Medievalism in English Canadian Literature (Boydell, 2020)
claims.quote: fantasy literature as one of many forms of recalling the Middle Ages

claims.feature: other: memory as the shape of the record
claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun takes David W. Marshall's remark that medievalism interrogates how groups, individuals or eras remember the Middle Ages as her starting point.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "Remembering the Romance", in M. J. Toswell (ed.), Medievalism in English Canadian Literature (Boydell, 2020)
claims.quote: medievalism interrogates how different groups, individuals, or eras

claims.claim: Kay names the ripple effects of the An Lushan Rebellion, rather than the events themselves, as part of what drew him to Tang China.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay interviewed by Sandra Alvarez, Medievalists.net (2016)
claims.quote: the colossal scale and consequence (through ripple effects)
claims.page: answer on which place he most enjoyed researching

claims.claim: Labrousse-Marchau argues that across Fionavar, Tigana and A Song for Arbonne the supernatural recedes until reality is disenchanted and the gods have left.
claims.source: Nathalie Labrousse-Marchau, "A Song for Arbonne: De-romanticised fantasy", trans. Francois Vincent (BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: Reality has become disenchanted. The gods have left.
claims.page: second section, on magic in A Song for Arbonne

claims.feature: other: moral ambiguity instead of good and evil
claims.claim: Labrousse-Marchau argues Kay refuses the good-and-evil dichotomy usual in the genre, binding shadow and light together.
claims.source: Nathalie Labrousse-Marchau, "A Song for Arbonne: De-romanticised fantasy", trans. Francois Vincent (BrightWeavings)
claims.quote: The shadows are inextricably linked to the light

claims.claim: The Siourbas chapter's full title names two works, Kay's Tigana and Randy Bradshaw's The Song Spinner, and it runs to eight pages.
claims.source: Project MUSE record for Worlds of Wonder, ed. Leroux and La Bossiere (University of Ottawa Press, 2004)
claims.quote: Kay's Tigana and Randy Bradshaw's The Song Spinner

claims.feature: other: fantasy as a method for history
claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun describes Kay's characteristic historical fantasy as grounded in history while using fantastic elements to detach the past from its particular settings.
claims.source: Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, "King Arthur and Imagined Indians", in Studies in Medievalism XXXIV (Boydell, 2025)
claims.quote: detach the past from its particular settings

verdicts.trueWording: between story as represented in history and story as transformed by fantasy
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture of the Questia preview reached and read directly. The quoted phrase appears word for word in the opening Article excerpt paragraph, in a sentence about Kay being fascinated with the multiplicity of story and the negotiations between new stories and old ones. Byline 'By Wolfe, Gary K.' and the JFA 20.2 Spring 2009 masthead are on the page; p. 238 is not shown on the preview but is not a limb of the claim sentence.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'the ICFA audience' - the page never names ICFA or the International Conference on the Fantastic in the Arts
verdicts.trueWording: a defense of fantasy literature as a way of addressing history
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture reached and read directly. The quotation is verbatim, in the sentence where Kay says he will 'connect this to' that defence, immediately after stating his privacy-and-autonomy thesis, so the privacy-to-fantasy limb is fully supported. The venue is given only circumstantially: he addresses 'guests of honor' alongside Farah Mendlesohn and Christine Mains, with a nod to 'spring training here in Florida'. grep for ICFA, IAFA and 'international conference' on the fetched page returns zero hits, so the ICFA identification is an inference, not the page's wording.

verdicts.trueWording: This is nonsense, and it is pervasive
verdicts.note: brightweavings.com/privacy/ fetched live (HTTP 200) and read in full. The page quotes a New York Times line on Oates's Blonde about a novel giving 'her interior world', then asks what has happened when someone suggests a novel gives the inner world of a real person, and answers with the quoted sentence. Quotation verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the absence of a record, offers license or opportunity
verdicts.note: Same live page, the Alias Grace passage. Kay quotes Atwood's fear of a biscuit box of Grace Marks letters, then draws the implication in the quoted words, and immediately contrasts Findley on Jung and Johnson on Smallwood, where the documented existence of a well-known subject is instead seen as 'actually conferring' licence. Both limbs supported verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Shouldn't we care what is real and what is made up?
verdicts.note: Same live page. The question is verbatim. It directly follows two reviewer remarks Kay sets side by side and asks the reader to pause over: the Calgary Herald on Johnson's Colony, whose reviewer says 'I don't care' how factual the novel is, and the New York Times on Blonde. The plural 'reviewers' is carried by that pair.

Same live page. The phrase is verbatim in the sentence saying that, with all the variations of purpose and craft, what we see in all of these works is that expanded perception. It sums up the run of novels by Findley, Johnson, Ondaatje, Atwood, Oates, Cunningham, DeLillo, Doctorow and Duffy, and sits immediately before the closing return to Yogi Berra, exactly as the claim's page field says.

verdicts.trueWording: the injury caused by seeing cannot be measured
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture of the JFA version reached and read. The rabbinical passage is quoted verbatim in the clause naming the unmeasurable injury. The societal-standard limb is supported by the surrounding sentences: the anxiety was 'judged worth assuaging by that society', the breach could not be permitted by the individual, and the intrusion was 'an offense against society, how it defined itself'.

verdicts.trueWording: All three of them strongly emphasize the transitory nature of things
verdicts.note: The repository PDF is an 18-page image-only Konica Minolta scan with no text layer (pdftotext yielded 18 bytes), so I rendered it at 250 dpi and OCRed every page with tesseract. On the page whose printed folio reads 222, under the running head 'Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun', the three sayings are set out as a labelled list - Asharite (109), Kindath (109), Jaddite (110) - followed immediately by the quoted sentence. Quotation verbatim; both limbs and the page number confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: fantasy literature as one of many forms of recalling the Middle Ages
verdicts.note: The identifier URL returns HTTP 301; following the redirect to the Cambridge Core chapter landing page gave the full chapter Summary. The quoted phrase appears verbatim in a sentence saying we can see fantasy literature that way 'in contemporary culture'. Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun is named as chapter author on the page and the range is given as pp. 155-171, consistent with a p. 155 opening.

verdicts.trueWording: medievalism interrogates how different groups, individuals, or eras
verdicts.note: Same Cambridge Core Summary. The Marshall quotation continues past the claim's fragment to 'remember the Middle Ages', is attributed on the page to David W. Marshall's introduction to a collection on the Middle Ages in popular culture, and the next sentence calls his observation 'an inspiring starting point'. Quotation verbatim; the starting-point limb is the page's own word.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'rather than the events themselves' - Kay names the rebellion's colossal scale alongside its consequence, not consequence instead of the events
verdicts.trueWording: colossal scale and consequence (through ripple effects)
verdicts.note: medievalists.net fetched live (HTTP 200) and read directly. Answering which place he most enjoyed researching, Kay says he found Tang China mesmerizing partly because of the poets and partly because of the quoted 'scale and consequence' of the An Lushan Rebellion. The quotation and the 'part of what drew him' limb are exact, but the source couples scale with consequence rather than setting ripple effects against the events, so the contrastive limb is the claim's own addition.

verdicts.trueWording: Reality has become disenchanted. The gods have left.
verdicts.note: brightweavings.com/nath_arbonne/ fetched live (HTTP 200) and read in full; the page credits Nathalie Labrousse-Marchau, translated by Francois Vincent. The two sentences are verbatim at the close of the paragraph tracing the recession: in Fionavar gods are present and magic permeates everything; in Tigana 'the gods are far off' and magic must be invoked at the cost of two fingers; in A Song for Arbonne 'the break is complete', with no magic and gods reduced to focal points for faith.

verdicts.trueWording: The shadows are inextricably linked to the light
verdicts.note: Same live page, penultimate paragraph. The sentence before the quotation says that with Kay we will not find the good-and-evil dichotomy 'so frequently employed in typical fantasy', and the quoted sentence continues 'and the light to the shadows'. Quotation verbatim; both the genre-refusal limb and the binding-together limb are the page's own wording.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the attribution to Siourbas - the MUSE table of contents lists chapter titles and page ranges only, with no author names
verdicts.trueWording: Kay's Tigana and Randy Bradshaw's The Song Spinner
verdicts.note: muse.jhu.edu/book/6623 fetched live (HTTP 200) and read directly. The table of contents carries the chapter title 'More Than Just Survival: The Successful Quest for Voice in' the two named works, with 'pp. 73-80', so the two-work limb is verbatim and the eight-page limb is exact. But grep for 'Siourbas' returns zero hits in both the rendered text and the raw HTML: every entry renders as a bare h3 title plus a page div, with the .toc .entry .author slot empty, so this page cannot confirm who wrote the chapter.

verdicts.trueWording: detach the past from its particular settings
verdicts.note: Cambridge Core page fetched live (HTTP 200) and read directly; Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun is named as chapter author and the range given as pp. 174-191. The chapter Summary says Kay has accustomed readers to a form of historical fantasy 'grounded in history' that uses the fantastic to detach the past from its particular settings 'and give it a more universal feel'. Quotation verbatim and every limb supported. The wording sits in the Cambridge Core abstract rather than in body text of p. 174.
